title: Clean Architecture & Hexagonal in Go — Revision

sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: As Go services grow beyond a few handlers, architectural discipline becomes critical to maintainability. Clean Architecture and its close cousin Hexagonal (Ports & Adapters) provide a layering model where domain logic is isolated from infrastructure — database, HTTP, message brokers — through interface boundaries. Interviewers at senior and staff level probe this module to see whether you can decompose a feature across layers, wire dependencies with tools like Google Wire or Uber Fx, and understand CQRS and event-driven patterns. The ability to articulate why these boundaries exist (testability, replaceability, independent evolution) marks you as someone who thinks beyond getting the feature shipped.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body: Clean Architecture in Go maps to four concentric package layers: domain (entities, value objects, domain services, no imports from outer layers), usecase/application (orchestrates domain objects, depends on repository interfaces), infrastructure (implements repository interfaces: Postgres, Redis, Kafka), and delivery (HTTP handlers, gRPC handlers, CLI commands). The Dependency Rule: source code dependencies point inward only; outer layers depend on inner layers, never the reverse. Hexagonal uses Ports (interfaces) and Adapters (implementations) — primary adapters drive the application (HTTP server calls the service interface), secondary adapters are driven by the application (service interface calls the repository). Wire and Fx provide compile-time and runtime dependency injection respectively, wiring the whole graph of constructors without manual hand-rolling.

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body: 1. Dependency Rule — domain knows nothing about HTTP, Postgres, or Kafka; only outer rings import inner rings. 2. Package layout — cmd/ (entry points), internal/domain/, internal/usecase/, internal/repository/, internal/handler/, pkg/ (shared libs). 3. Hexagonal primary adapter — e.g. chi router calling usecase.CreateOrder(); the HTTP concern is fully encapsulated in the adapter. 4. Hexagonal secondary adapter — e.g. PostgresOrderRepository implementing domain.OrderRepository interface. 5. Wire (Google) — compile-time DI: write provider functions, run wire.go generation; type-safe, catches missing dependencies at compile time. 6. Fx (Uber) — runtime DI: register constructors with fx.Provide, run with fx.New; more dynamic, supports lifecycle hooks (OnStart, OnStop). 7. CQRS — separate command (write) model from query (read) model; commands mutate state and emit events; queries read from optimised projections. 8. Event-driven Go — domain events published via an in-process EventBus or outbox pattern to Kafka; subscribers react without direct coupling.

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body: Q: What is the Dependency Rule in Clean Architecture and why does it matter? — All source code dependencies point inward (toward domain); domain code can be tested with no database, no HTTP server; you can swap Postgres for SQLite in tests or swap REST for gRPC in delivery without touching domain logic. Q: How does Hexagonal Architecture differ from layered architecture? — Hexagonal focuses on ports (interfaces) and adapters (implementations), making it explicit which external systems are being adapted; traditional layered architecture is a stack where each layer calls the layer below. Q: How does Google Wire differ from Uber Fx? — Wire is a code-generation tool: it reads provider declarations and generates a wire_gen.go with explicit constructor calls — fully visible, no reflection. Fx is a runtime dependency injection container using reflection; it supports lifecycle hooks and is easier to use dynamically. Q: What is the outbox pattern and why is it used with event-driven Go services? — Publishing a domain event and writing to the database in two separate operations can fail atomically; the outbox pattern writes the event to an outbox table in the same transaction, and a separate relay process reads and publishes it to Kafka, guaranteeing at-least-once delivery. Q: What is CQRS and when is it worth the complexity? — Separate write model (commands, validation, business rules) from read model (queries, projections, aggregations); valuable when write and read performance or data shapes diverge significantly; overhead is not worth it for simple CRUD services.

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: "For services beyond a few hundred lines I adopt a Clean Architecture layout: domain types and interfaces in internal/domain with zero external imports, use-case orchestration in internal/usecase depending only on domain interfaces, infrastructure implementations in internal/repository and internal/messaging, and HTTP handlers in internal/handler. The payoff is that every use case has pure unit tests with mock repositories — no database, no HTTP server needed. I wire the whole graph with Google Wire because the generated wire_gen.go makes the dependency tree explicit and catches missing providers at compile time. For services that have clearly divergent read and write patterns — like a reporting dashboard alongside a transactional write path — I introduce CQRS: commands go through the use case and emit domain events; read models are maintained by event handlers and optimised for their specific query shapes. For async event publishing I use the outbox pattern so the event and the database write are atomic — I never fire-and-forget to Kafka outside a transaction."
